title: 8  Measures of Location and Spread (and Other Parameters of Probability Distributions)
text:
8.2 Variance and standard deviation
Like the sample variance computed with observed data, the variance of a random variable measures the average squared deviation from the mean. As with the mean, the average is weighted by each outcome’s probability.

Definition 8.2: Variance and standard deviation of a random variable
The variance of a random variable \(X\) with mean \(\mu\) is the probability-weighted average of squared deviations from the mean. For a discrete random variable with possible outcomes \(x_1, \dots, x_k\),
\[
\text{Var}(X) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \Pr(X = x_i)\,(x_i - \mu)^2.
\]
We write \(\sigma^2 = \text{Var}(X)\). The standard deviation is its square root, \(SD(X) = \sigma = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}\). Just like its sample counterpart, the standard deviation is in the same units as \(X\) and can be interpreted as a typical distance from the mean.


In words: the variance is the expected squared distance between the random variable and its mean — how wrong, on the squared-error scale, we expect to be if we predict \(X\) by \(\mu\). For the 16% loan, the payoff sits $1,400 above its mean of $10,200 when the loan is repaid and $4,200 below it on default, so
\[
\text{Var}(X) = 0.75 \times (1{,}400)^2 + 0.25 \times (-4{,}200)^2 = 5{,}880{,}000,
\]
and taking the square root brings us back to dollars: \(SD(X)\) = $2,425. The standard deviation combines the two possible deviations — $1,400 when the loan is repaid and $4,200 when it defaults — into one probability-weighted measure of spread. The interpretation is the one we built for data in Section 3.2: a bigger standard deviation means a less predictable outcome.

Notation 8.1: Random variables, parameters, and statistics

Capital letters name random variables (\(X\), \(Y\), \(D\)).
Lowercase letters name particular values they might take (\(x\), \(y\)).
Greek letters name parameters of a true probability or population distribution: \(\mu\) for its mean, \(\sigma^2\) for its variance, \(\sigma\) for its standard deviation.
Lowercase Latin letters denote quantities computed from a single observed sample: \(\bar{x}\) for a sample mean, \(s^2\) and \(s\) for a sample variance and standard deviation. They are lowercase because they are already-observed numbers, not random.
Uppercase Latin letters like \(\bar X\) denote a quantity computed on a random sample — in this case, the mean of that random sample. They’re random variables because they’re uncertain due to the random sampling. We’ll work with \(\bar X\) when we average random variables later in the course.

When you see a Greek letter, it refers to something unknown we’re trying to estimate. When you see a Latin letter, we have computed it (or could compute it) from data. Lowercase Latin letters (\(\bar{x}\), \(s\)) are numbers we computed from our observed sample; uppercase Latin letters like \(\bar{X}\) are random variables, because the samples they depend on are random.



8.2.1 Variance/Standard deviation measure unpredictability (risk)
As in Section 3.2, the spread of a probability distribution represents unpredictability or risk. The standard deviation is high when there is substantial probability placed on outcomes that are far from the expected value (the mean). Here are two hypothetical $10,000 loans with the same expected profit but different risk profiles. Both assume that the lender recovers $6,000 if the borrower defaults:

Loan A and Loan B have the same expected profit of $320, so expected value alone cannot choose between them. Their standard deviations can: $2,160 for Loan A against $1,440 for Loan B. Loan A places more probability on outcomes far from that shared average in both directions, which is what a lender means by calling it the riskier loan. Writing many loans like either one is profitable in the long run, provided defaults are close to independent — but a lender choosing between them gets one draw. At the same expected profit, a risk-averse lender takes Loan B.


Both loans’ long-run profitability rests on defaults being at least close to independent: one borrower’s failure tells us nothing about the others. We’ll define independence carefully later in the course.
The same comparison drives how investors think about other investments. Two stocks can have return distributions with the same expected return but very different standard deviations; Figure 8.2 shows such a pair.

text:
8.3 Quantiles and the IQR
Percentiles and quantiles carry over from data to distributions the same way. The \(p\)-th quantile of a distribution is the smallest value where the cumulative probability reaches or exceeds \(p\). For example: the median of a distribution is its 0.5 quantile: the smallest value where the cumulative probability reaches or exceeds 0.50. For our house price model, the median is $488,127:








Figure 8.3: The median of the Austin price model. Left: the density with exactly half its area shaded, up to the median. Right: the CDF crossing cumulative probability 0.50 at the same price.





Just as we discussed in Section 3.1, the median can be a more robust measure of center than the mean for a skewed probability distribution; in the model above, the mean price is $546,458, which is $58,331 above the median. The mean is pulled up by the long right tail of the distribution, just as it was in the observed data.
For a continuous distribution, we can read it off the CDF by finding where the curve crosses height \(p\). The median is the 0.5 quantile, and the interquartile range is the distance between the 0.25 and 0.75 quantiles, a spread measure in the units of the variable that ignores the tails entirely.








Figure 8.4: Reading quantiles off the CDF of the Austin price model. Horizontal lines at cumulative probabilities 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75 cross the curve above the model’s quartiles and median; the distance between the two outer drop-lines is the IQR.





For the price model, the quartiles land at $354,282 and $672,536, so the IQR is $318,254: under this model, the middle half of future sales falls in a band about $318,254 wide. Quantiles also answer tail questions directly — a seller wondering “what price will I beat with probability 0.75?” wants the 0.25 quantile, not the mean.

title: 8  Measures of Location and Spread (and Other Parameters of Probability Distributions)
text:
8.4 Shifting and scaling
Linear transformations of random variables act just like linear transformations applied to columns in our datasets:






NoteMean, median, and standard deviation of \(aX + b\)



If \(X\) is a random variable with mean \(E[X] = \mu\) and standard deviation \(SD(X) = \sigma\), and \(a\) and \(b\) are known constants, then \(Y = aX + b\) has
\[
E[Y] = a\,\mu + b, \qquad \text{median}(Y) = a\,\text{median}(X) + b,
\]
\[
SD(Y) = |a|\,\sigma, \qquad Var(Y) = a^2\,\sigma^2.
\]
Adding \(b\) shifts the center and leaves the spread alone; multiplying by \(a\) scales both the center and the spread (and the spread doesn’t care about the sign of \(a\)).


These are exactly the same rules we encountered for the sample mean, median, and variance/SD in Section 4.1.
The profit on our 16% loan is \(X - 10{,}000\), so its mean is $10,200 \(-\) $10,000 = $200 and its standard deviation is exactly the payoff’s $2,424.87 — shifting can’t make an uncertain payoff any more or less predictable. Scaling Loan B’s $10,000 principal up to $100,000 sets \(a = 10\): expected profit rises to $3,200, and the standard deviation rises right along with it to $14,400.
We standardize a random variable by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation, producing a new random variable with mean 0 and standard deviation 1:
\[
Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}.
\]
The new random variable \(Z\) measures how many standard deviations \(X\) sits from its own mean. A realized value of \(Z\) is a z-score and just like in Section 4.2 it measures the size of an observed difference relative to a typical difference, as measured by standard deviation.

title: 8  Measures of Location and Spread (and Other Parameters of Probability Distributions)
text:
8.5 Continuous random variables
The expected value, variance, and standard deviation are all interpreted the same way for a continuous random variable, but the formulas change from sums to integrals:

Technical detail 8.1: Mean and variance as integrals
If a continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \(f(x)\) then
\[
E[X] = \int x \, f(x) \, dx, \qquad
\text{Var}(X) = \int (x - \mu)^2 \, f(x) \, dx,
\]
and \(SD(X) = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}\) as always. The integrals play the role the sums played for discrete random variables: they average over every possible outcome, weighting by the density instead of by individual probabilities. The mean and variance of the Austin price model come from integrals of exactly this kind, and software evaluates them.


The mean is still the long-run average, and the standard deviation still measures how far outcomes typically stray from it. The Austin price model’s standard deviation is the square root of its variance, while its median and quartiles come from the CDF.

title: 9  The Normal Distribution
text:
9.1 The probability density function
This chapter introduces one of the most important families of continuous probability distributions: the normal distribution.
A normal distribution’s density is the symmetric bell-shaped curve in Figure 9.1. Changing \(\mu\) slides the curve left or right without altering its shape; changing \(\sigma^2\) stretches or squeezes it without moving the center.
Figure 9.1: Three normal densities. Increasing the mean from 0 to 2 slides the density to the right without changing its shape; increasing the variance from 1 to 4 spreads it out without moving its center.
Since the normal distribution is symmetric, its mean and median are the same.
A shifted and scaled normal random variable is still normal: if \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then \(Y = aX + b\) follows another normal distribution with mean and variance given by the shifting-and-scaling rules from Section 8.4: \(N(a\mu + b,\; a^2\sigma^2)\).

title: 9  The Normal Distribution
text:
Definition 9.1: Normal distribution
The normal distribution (also known as the Gaussian distribution) is the symmetric continuous distribution governed entirely by two parameters: a mean \(\mu\) and a variance \(\sigma^2\). The mean locates the center of the density curve and the variance controls how wide it is.

Details and formulas
The density is
\[
f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}
       \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).
\]
The exponent is a squared z-score, so the density falls off with the square of the distance from \(\mu\) measured in standard deviations, and the leading constant is whatever makes the total area equal one. We never evaluate this by hand — software computes normal densities, probabilities, and quantiles.







Notation 9.1: \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\)
We write
\[
X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)
\]
to say that the random variable \(X\) follows a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\); the “\(\sim\)” reads “is distributed as.”
The second parameter is the variance, not the standard deviation. Most software for computing normal probabilities, densities, and quantiles takes the mean and standard deviation as arguments instead, so the two conventions have to be kept straight when moving between a written model and code.

title: 9  The Normal Distribution
text:
9.2 Computing probabilities
To illustrate probability computations with the normal distribution we’ll build a model for weekly S&P 500 returns, using the historical mean and standard deviation as the parameters: \(R \sim N(0.0047, 0.0212^2)\) — a mean weekly return of about 0.47% and a standard deviation of about 2.12%. Figure 9.2 plots the estimated model over the data.








Figure 9.2: Weekly S&P 500 returns (density-scaled histogram) with the fitted normal model overlaid. The fitted density tracks the data well through the middle; the most extreme weeks sit a little further out than the model expects.





To be clear: Weekly returns are not literally normal — a return can’t fall below \(-100\%\), and real markets tend to produce more extreme outcomes than a normal distribution would give. What we are claiming (for now!) is that the normal distribution is a good enough approximation: close enough to the true distribution, in the region we care about, that probability statements computed from it are useful. That’s the case for any model, and to the extent we can, we should check whether our modeling assumptions are supported or not by the data available to us. We’ll do that below.
With that model in hand we can compute any probabilities of interest as areas under the curve.

A losing week. \(\Pr(R < 0) = 0.41\). Even in a market that drifts upward on average, the model gives roughly a 41% chance that any given week loses money.
A bad week. \(\Pr(R < -3\%) = 0.05\) — about one week in every 20.
A quiet week. \(\Pr(-1.5\% < R < 1.5\%) = 0.51\).









Figure 9.3: Four probability statements as areas under the fitted normal model for weekly returns. Each panel’s title reports the probability; the shaded region is the corresponding area.





A few more examples reinforce our basic probability rules, and how they are used to compute probabilities for normal random variables:

A non-losing week. \(\Pr(R \geq 0) = 0.59 = 1-\Pr(R < 0)\).
A winning week. \(\Pr(R > 0) = \Pr(R \geq 0)\), because for a continuous distribution, \(\Pr(R = 0) = 0\) and \(\Pr(R \geq 0) = \Pr(R > 0) + \Pr(R = 0)\) since the two events are mutually exclusive.

We can evaluate any normal probability we like using our basic probability rules and software that can evaluate the normal CDF to compute the areas like we did above. (The same is true for any continuous probability distribution.) Sketching the areas can be useful practice until you get the hang of this.
For example, the interval probability \(\Pr(-1.5\% < R < 1.5\%)\) can be computed a few different ways: We can start by computing \(\Pr(R < 1.5\%)\) and then subtracting off \(\Pr(R < -1.5\%)\) to eliminate the tail area we didn’t want. Or we could recognize that \(\Pr(-1.5\% < R < 1.5\%) = 1 - [\Pr(R < -1.5\%) + \Pr(R > 1.5\%)]\), since \(R<-1.5\%\) and \(R>1.5\%\) are the two mutually exclusive ways to land outside the interval. Figure 9.4 sketches both routes.








Figure 9.4: Two routes to the same interval probability. Top row: start with everything below 1.5% and subtract the tail below -1.5%. Bottom row: start with total probability 1 and subtract the two tails outside the interval.

title: 9  The Normal Distribution
text:
9.3 The 68/95/99.7 rule
For normal distributions, three particular areas come up over and over: the probability that an outcome lands within one, two, or three standard deviations of the mean.

Definition 9.2: The 68/95/99.7 rule
If \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then approximately:

68% of the probability lies within one standard deviation of the mean, \(\mu \pm \sigma\).
95% lies within two standard deviations, \(\mu \pm 2\sigma\).
99.7% lies within three standard deviations, \(\mu \pm 3\sigma\).











Figure 9.5: The 68/95/99.7 rule on the weekly-returns model. Each horizontal bar spans the interval mu plus-or-minus 1, 2, or 3 standard deviations; the label above each bar is the proportion of outcomes landing inside that interval.





Applied to the returns model: about two weeks in three land between -1.6% and 2.6%; about 19 weeks in 20 land between -3.8% and 4.7%; and a week outside -5.9% to 6.8% should be a once-in-several-years event. The rule works in both directions. Given the parameters you can sketch the whole distribution in your head, and given an extreme outcome you can immediately place it: a \(-4\%\) week sits about two standard deviations below the mean, the kind of week you should expect about once a year (if there’s no dependence between consecutive weekly returns).

title: 9  The Normal Distribution
text:
9.4 Z-scores, again
Standardizing a normal random variable — \(Z = (X - \mu)/\sigma\) — produces the standard normal distribution \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\). Since \(Z\) now represents standard deviations from the mean, we know that if a random variable is normally distributed, we should see values more than 2 standard deviations from the mean about 5% of the time, and values more than 3 standard deviations from the mean about 0.3% of the time. Here z-scores tell us quite a bit about the associated probability of seeing an outcome at least as far from the mean as \(Z\) — but only because the random variable has a normal distribution.






WarningCommon mistake: Z-scores carry probabilities only for normal distributions



These probability statements attach to z-scores only when the underlying random variable is normal. For any distribution, a z-score still measures how many standard deviations an outcome sits from its mean — that much is pure arithmetic. But the translation from z-scores to probabilities depends entirely on the distribution’s shape. A z-score of 2.5 is a once-in-eighty event under a normal distribution; under a heavy-tailed one it might be a monthly occurrence.


The z-score restatement also gives us a quick model check. If weekly returns really follow our fitted normal, about 5% of weeks — five or so out of our 104 — should land more than two standard deviations from the mean. In the data, 6 weeks do: right in line. A handful of weeks land quite far out in the tails, and the tails are exactly where financial data tend to deviate from a normal model. Judging them by counting is crude; the next section builds a better diagnostic for checking normality (and more generally for comparing any two distributions).

title: 9  The Normal Distribution
text:
9.5 QQ plots: checking normality
In the last section we checked the returns model at a single quantile, counting the weeks that landed more than two standard deviations from the mean. A quantile-quantile (QQ) plot makes that kind of comparison at every quantile at once. If a variable has a normal distribution, after standardization we know the median should be close to zero, the 2.5th percentile should be about -2, the 97.5th percentile about +2, and so on. The QQ plot puts the theoretical normal quantile on the horizontal axis and the corresponding observed quantile on the vertical axis. If the data are truly close to normal, the points will trace out a straight line. Large departures from the line mean normality is questionable, and where the points bend away tells you how the data deviate. The examples below show the common patterns.
Figure 9.6 builds the plot up one quantile at a time, using our z-scored weekly returns. Each frame fixes a single percentile and asks where it lands in two distributions: in the data (the blue line, dropped onto the density-scaled histogram at top) and in a standard normal (the purple line, on the standard normal density below). That pair of quantiles — one observed, one theoretical — becomes a single point on the plot at right. Sweeping from the 1st percentile to the 99th plots one point per comparison, and the points trace out the QQ curve.






Figure 9.6: Building a QQ plot for the z-scored weekly returns. Each frame matches one percentile between the data (blue, top) and the standard normal (purple, bottom) and records the pair as a point on the right. The finished curve stays close to the 45-degree line, bending away only at the extreme quantiles.



Figure 9.7 runs four variables through the same comparison, each with its QQ plot beside a histogram of its z-scores.








Figure 9.7: Left column: QQ plots of the z-scored variables against the standard normal, so the reference line is the same 45-degree line in every panel. Right column: histograms of the same z-scores with the standard normal density overlaid. Hourly wages are a random subsample of 5,000 workers; daily electricity demand is the mean hourly DFW load for each day from 2016–2020.





Each panel revisits a distribution whose shape we already know from the data chapters. The market returns track the line closely, with the smallest and largest weeks pulling slightly away from it — the outlying weeks from the last section. In small datasets some variability at extreme quantiles is to be expected, but sustained deviations from the line are suspicious. For reference, here are QQ plots for a few randomly generated datasets of the same size as the S&P 500 data, each drawn from a standard normal distribution:








Figure 9.8: QQ plots for six simulated datasets of the same size as the returns data (n = 104), each drawn exactly from a normal distribution. Even perfectly normal data wobbles around the line at the extreme quantiles; deviations of this size are consistent with sampling variation.





Looking through the other examples, we see sustained deviations from normality. Hourly wages bow high above the line at the top: extreme earners are far larger than any normal distribution would produce — strong right skew. The flat run of identical points at the very top is a survey artifact, not a distributional shape: the largest reported earnings are capped at a common value. Taking logs — the transformation from Chapter 4 — pulls the wage points much closer to the line, but we still see some evidence of heavier tails than expected. Daily electricity demand flattens out at both ends of the line: its extremes are less extreme than a normal’s. The flat stretch of points cutting across the line in the middle of the panel is a different signal — many days pile up at similar loads, suggesting a mode or “shoulder” — and neither feature is consistent with a normal distribution.

Provenance. The data were scraped from Zillow by Eric Pierce and published on Kaggle in 2021. Coverage is limited to Austin, Texas residential listings with recorded sale prices. A.2 CPS ASEC Earnings
The Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) to the Current Population Survey (CPS) is a nationally representative household survey conducted each March by the U.S. Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics. It is one of the principal federal sources for data on annual earnings, employment, and hours worked in the United States. The survey covers civilian non-institutional residents and collects detailed information on labor force participation, earnings, education, and demographics.
This dataset contains information on wages, age, education, and gender for a subsample of prime-age, full-time, full-year wage earners extracted from the Current Population Survey (CPS). The CPS is the primary source for labor market data in the U.S.; its best-known use is in estimating the unemployment rate and related statistics. It is widely used in economics research, including studies of wage determination and human capital.
Each March the CPS includes the Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC), which collects detailed information on income, earnings, and work experience for the prior calendar year. The ASEC is the most comprehensive source of data on annual earnings in the U.S. This dataset was extracted from the 2023 CPS ASEC.
Resources:

CPS ASEC documentation (Census Bureau) – details about the survey design, target population, data collection, and variables available in the ASEC.
Mincer earnings function (Wikipedia) – this dataset is suitable for estimating the Mincer earnings function, a widely used model in labor economics that relates wages to schooling and experience.

Data were obtained via the cpsR R package, which queries the Census Bureau’s API and returns a tidy extract from the 2023 ASEC public-use microdata file. The underlying microdata represent civilian non-institutional respondents nationwide. No license restrictions apply to CPS public-use files; the data are freely available from the U.S. Census Bureau.

A.3 Weekly Asset Returns (2023–2025)
These data document weekly simple returns for 25 exchange-traded assets—individual equities, a sector ETF, bond ETFs, and a commodity ETF—alongside a contemporaneous weekly risk-free rate, covering the period September 30, 2023 to September 29, 2025. Prices are sourced from Yahoo Finance and converted to weekly simple returns using split- and dividend-adjusted closing prices. section: A.5 ERCOT Hourly Load and Temperature Panel
text:
A.5 ERCOT Hourly Load and Temperature Panel
These data were assembled to characterize the relationship between temperature and electricity demand in Texas. The panel links hourly zone-level load from ERCOT with hourly surface temperature observations from nearby weather stations, enabling temperature response functions to be estimated separately for each of ERCOT’s eight weather zones. Shaffer (2022) uses these data to examine how the load–temperature relationship changed over time, estimating the functions across rolling multi-year windows from 2002 through 2020.
Resources:

Article
Replication archive

Provenance. Load data originate from the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) and reflect hourly settlement-point electricity demand, in megawatts, for each of ERCOT’s eight weather zones from January 2002 through March 2021. Temperature data originate from NOAA’s Local Climatological Data (LCD) product, which reports hourly observations from Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) and Automated Weather Observing System (AWOS) stations. NOAA LCD reports dry-bulb temperature in degrees Fahrenheit for U.S. stations; the field name HourlyDryBulbTemperature is the exact column name used in LCD exports. One representative station was selected per ERCOT weather zone. The two sources are matched on datetime and zone. Large-scale load-shed events (outages) are flagged from ERCOT operating records to allow their exclusion from estimation. All data were curated by Blake Shaffer and are archived at the replication repository above. See Shaffer (2022) for the primary citation.

A.6 LendingClub Accepted Loans
LendingClub operated an online marketplace that matched individual borrowers with investors who funded loans in small fractional shares (“notes”). To let investors screen and price loans, the company published detailed loan-level records for every funded loan — borrower credit attributes recorded at origination together with the loan’s subsequent repayment history. These data are widely used to study consumer-credit default and loan pricing. This card documents a cleaned extract used to model loan charge-off and investor payoff.

Provenance. A.7 SAP Customer ROE
In 2005 SAP began running advertisements claiming that companies running SAP software are 32% more profitable than companies that don’t, citing a study it had commissioned from Stratascope Inc. that was never released for public scrutiny (Carr 2005). In March 2006 the technology analyst firm Nucleus Research pushed back with a research note titled “SAP customers are 20 percent less profitable than their peers.” Nucleus compiled the publicly traded companies appearing on SAP’s own web site — 81 firms — looked up each one’s return on equity (ROE) from published financial data, and compared it with the average ROE of the firm’s industry. The average across the 81 firms was 12.6%, against an industry-average benchmark of 15.7%. These data are used in the notes to estimate the mean ROE among SAP customers, to test hypotheses about both companies’ claims, and to examine what a non-random sample can and cannot support.
Resources:

Nucleus Research note G12 (PDF)
Rough Type on the ad campaign
Rough Type on the Stratascope study

Provenance. The figures are transcribed from Table 1 of Nucleus Research (2006) (Nucleus Research note G12, March 2006), which lists each company with its SAP solution(s), industry, ROE, and industry-average ROE. Nucleus reports gathering the ROE figures from Bloomberg and the industry averages from Hoovers via Yahoo! Finance. The note itself circulates today courtesy of Oracle — an SAP competitor with an obvious interest in its conclusions — though Nucleus states the analysis was conducted independently and not commissioned by any company. The one derived column, roe_diff, was added for this book.
A caution on sampling. These 81 firms are not a random sample of SAP customers: they are the publicly traded companies SAP itself chose to feature on its web site. The inference chapter leans on this fact — analyses of these data describe SAP’s showcased customers, not SAP customers in general.

A.9 Bloom, Han & Liang (2024) Hybrid WFH Experiment
Bloom, Han & Liang (2024) ran a six-month randomized controlled trial at a Chinese technology company in 2021–2022, randomly assigning 1,612 graduate-educated employees to a hybrid work-from-home schedule (two days per week at home) or a full-time in-person control condition. The study examines whether hybrid WFH affects employee retention, job performance, promotion rates, and subjective productivity beliefs. The three datasets documented here cover the paper’s core outcomes: employee attrition, daily lines of code written by software engineers, and manager perceptions of WFH’s effect on productivity.
Resources:

Article
Replication archive

Provenance. Data were collected by the research team of Nicholas Bloom, Ruobing Han, and James Liang as part of a pre-registered field experiment conducted at a large Chinese technology firm between July 2021 and June 2022. The replication archive, including the datasets documented here, is deposited at the Harvard Dataverse (doi:10.7910/DVN/6X4ZZL) and is freely available under a Creative Commons CC BY 4.0 licence. The original article was published open-access in Nature in June 2024. See Bloom et al. (2024) for the primary citation.

Attrition
The attrition dataset (attrition.csv) contains one row per employee (n = 1,612) and records whether each individual left the firm during the study period, together with the key subgroup characteristics used to stratify comparisons in the paper.

Because it takes only these two values, the group mean equals the attrition rate expressed as a percentage. Outcome variable in all attrition analyses.


treat
Categorical
Control / Treatment
Experimental assignment. “Treatment” employees followed a hybrid WFH schedule (two days per week working from home); “Control” employees worked in-person full-time. The key independent variable.


role
Categorical
Manager / Non-manager
Whether the employee held a managerial position. Used to stratify attrition comparisons; the paper finds that the quit-rate reduction from hybrid WFH is concentrated among non-managers.


male
Categorical
Male / Female
Employee gender. Used to stratify attrition comparisons; the paper finds a significant reduction in quit rates for female employees.


live_far
Categorical
Commute ≤ 90 mins / Commute > 90 mins
Commute-distance indicator based on round-trip commute time, with the sample median (90 minutes) as the threshold. Employees above the median are classified as long commuters. Used to stratify attrition comparisons; the paper finds a significant quit-rate reduction for long commuters.








Productivity
The productivity dataset (codelines.csv) contains one row per engineer-day observation (n ≈ 95,500) and records the daily lines of code written by software engineer employees, together with several log-transformed versions used in the analysis. Zero values are common, reflecting non-coding days.

The perceptions dataset (perceptions.csv) contains one row per survey respondent-wave observation (n = 2,660) and records employees’ self-reported beliefs about how working from home affects their productivity, collected at baseline (before the policy) and endline (after six months). A.10 Household economics (SHED)
The Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking (SHED) is an annual survey of U.S. adults conducted since 2013 by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. It measures how households assess their own finances and the broader economy, alongside employment, income, housing, and demographic characteristics. The course extract shed_2025.csv covers the 2025 wave: 12,934 respondents, drawn from a probability-based online panel designed to be representative of the U.S. adult population.
Resources:

SHED — Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
Public-use data and codebooks

Provenance. The public-use 2025 microdata file was downloaded from the Board’s SHED data page. As a work of the federal government, the file is in the public domain and may be copied and distributed without permission; the Board requests citation. The course extract keeps nine columns from the original 380, renames them to snake_case, and changes no values. Survey weights are not carried in the extract; course examples report unweighted proportions, which on the extract’s variables differ from weighted ones by less than a percentage point. Respondents rate every retained item on a forced-choice basis, so the extract has no missing values and no “don’t know” category.

A.11 Course Evaluations and Instructor Appearance
Do better-looking instructors get better teaching evaluations? Hamermesh and Parker (2005) collected student course evaluations for 463 course sections taught by 94 instructors at the University of Texas at Austin between 2000 and 2002, along with a measure of each instructor’s physical attractiveness: a panel of six students rated a photograph of each instructor, and the ratings were averaged and normalized. Hamermesh and Parker found that instructors rated as better looking receive systematically higher evaluations. In the regression chapters these data serve as a running multiple-regression example — in particular, whether the association between beauty ratings and evaluation scores survives adjusting for instructor age and other course and instructor characteristics.
Resources:

Article
AER package on CRAN (distributes this extract as TeachingRatings)

Provenance. The data were collected by Daniel Hamermesh and Amy Parker for Hamermesh and Parker (2005). Each row is one course section; instructor characteristics (age, gender, beauty rating, and so on) repeat across an instructor’s sections, indexed by prof. The beauty score is the average of six student panelists’ ratings of the instructor’s photograph, normalized to have mean zero across instructors (standard deviation about 0.79 in this file). This extract is the widely used teaching version of the data that circulates with Stock and Watson’s econometrics text and is distributed in the R package AER as TeachingRatings; the one column not in that distribution, generation, is a recode of age added for teaching purposes. See Hamermesh and Parker (2005) for the primary citation.
